opus-5.5.text:
I'd be pretty cautious about drawing strong conclusions from that. One of the more consistent things we've seen is that transfer and generalization get a lot better as models get bigger. Small models tend to treat different domains, or different ways of phrasing the same thing, as more or less separate. They kind of memorize each one on its own terms. Larger models seem to build more shared internal representations, so something learned in one setting is more likely to show up in another.

So if a GPT-2-sized model fails to transfer across domains, my default reading is that this is weak evidence about what a much larger model would do. It might just mean the small model doesn't have the capacity to find the common structure. There are a bunch of examples where an ability barely shows up at small scale and then becomes fairly robust once you scale up. Multilingual transfer is a good one. If you fine-tune on English data, a large model will often apply that behavior in other languages, which a small model does much less reliably.

That said, I wouldn't say small-scale experiments are useless. If you see positive transfer at small scale, that's a decent sign it'll hold or get stronger at larger scale. The asymmetry is that negative results at small scale are much less informative. If you really care about the answer, you probably want to run a scaling study: test at several model sizes and see whether the transfer effect is trending up. If it's growing with scale, you can extrapolate with some confidence. If it's flat, that's more concerning. But one data point at GPT-2 scale wouldn't make me confident either way.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-2-scale failure is weak evidence about a much larger model and that one small-scale result is not conclusive.

r002.rationale: It says larger models seem to build more shared internal representations, making cross-setting transfer more likely.

r003.rationale: It explains that small models may treat domains separately and memorize each one on its own terms.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd be pretty cautious about drawing strong conclusions from that. The history of the field is full of cases where something didn't work at small scale and then suddenly started working once the model got big enough. Few-shot learning is the classic example: with GPT-2 you'd see hints of it, but it was weak and unreliable, and it was easy to look at that and conclude in-context learning just wasn't a viable path. Then GPT-3 came along and it was clearly a real capability.

So a negative result on transfer at the GPT-2 scale mostly tells me that transfer doesn't work at that scale. It's weak evidence about what happens at a hundred times the compute. The reason is that a lot of these abilities seem to depend on the model having learned some shared, more abstract representation of the underlying structure across domains, and small models often don't have the capacity or the data to form that. They end up learning more surface-level, domain-specific features, and of course those don't transfer. A larger model trained on more diverse data has much more incentive to find representations that are reused across tasks, because that's the compressive, efficient thing to do.

What I'd actually want to look at is the trend rather than a single point. If you can run the experiment at a few scales, say GPT-2 small, medium, large, XL, and transfer gets monotonically better even if it's still bad in absolute terms, that's fairly encouraging. If it's flat across all of those, that's more worrying, though even then I wouldn't fully rule it out, because some things really do look like phase transitions on a given metric. Often that's an artifact of the metric, by the way. If you measure with something smoother, like log probability of the right answer rather than exact-match accuracy, the capability usually looks like it's been gradually emerging the whole time.

The other thing I'd check is whether the failure is about the model or about the setup. Is the small model failing to transfer because the knowledge isn't there, or because it can't follow the format, or it's overfitting the fine-tuning data? Sometimes a small model actually has the relevant knowledge but doesn't express it, and some change to the training procedure or the prompting unlocks it. Those failure modes get much less severe as you scale up.

So my overall interpretation would be: a small-scale negative result should lower your confidence a bit, but not that much, and you should go looking for the scaling trend before concluding anything. And honestly, the prior from the last several years is that if a capability is at all plausible, it'll show up at some scale.

r001.rationale: The response says a GPT-2-scale negative result is weak evidence about larger scales and should not rule out transfer at GPT-4 scale.

r002.rationale: It proposes that larger models are more likely to learn shared, abstract representations reused across domains.

r003.rationale: It identifies overfitting the fine-tuning data as a possible reason a small model fails to transfer, which is a form of excessive reliance on training-specific patterns.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t take that as strong evidence that transfer won’t work in a GPT-4-sized model. The smaller model might simply not have the capabilities or representations needed to transfer what it learned to the other domain. So you’d want to distinguish a failure of the training method from a limitation of the underlying model.

I’d look at how transfer changes with scale. If it starts working better as the models get larger, that’s suggestive. But even if you see no transfer at the smaller scales, I’d be cautious about extrapolating that negative result. Ideally, you’d test it on a model that actually has the relevant capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says a GPT-2-sized model’s failure is not strong evidence transfer will fail at GPT-4 scale and cautions against extrapolating that negative result.

r002.rationale: It says larger models may have the capabilities or representations needed to transfer, but does not state that they may learn better shared representations than smaller models.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest memorization as a possible explanation for the smaller model’s transfer failure.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t take that as very strong evidence that it won’t work in the larger model. The smaller model might just not have the capabilities you need for transfer. If it hasn’t learned the relevant concepts in both domains, you wouldn’t necessarily expect training in one to affect its behavior in the other.

So I’d want to look at how transfer changes with scale, and whether the model can actually do the underlying tasks. A negative result at GPT-2 scale is useful, but it doesn’t settle what happens at GPT-4 scale.
